opus-5.5.text:
I think replicating something like Operator is hard, but the difficulty isn't where many people assume. A demo is not that hard. You can wrap a strong vision-language model, have it look at screenshots, output clicks and keystrokes, and on a few hand-picked tasks it will look impressive. Many teams in China can build that in a few weeks.

The real challenge is making it actually work, robustly, on long and messy real-world tasks. I'd break it into a few layers.

The first is the base model. An agent like this needs strong visual grounding: understanding a web page or GUI precisely, knowing which element to click, reading small text, handling pop-ups. It also needs strong reasoning to plan over many steps and recover when something goes wrong. Chinese base models have caught up quickly on language and reasoning, but fine-grained multimodal grounding and long-horizon decision-making are still areas where the gap is real.

The second, and I think the more fundamental one, is reinforcement learning. Operator isn't just a model plus a prompt. To get reliability, you have to train the model in interactive environments, let it try, fail, and learn from outcomes. That means building large numbers of realistic environments, such as browsers, websites, and apps, where you can run thousands of rollouts in parallel, define rewards, and verify whether a task really succeeded. This is heavy infrastructure work. Rollouts are slow, environments are flaky, websites change, rewards are hard to specify. Agentic RL at scale is a systems problem as much as an algorithm problem, and not many teams have invested deeply there yet.

The third is data and task design. You need a distribution of tasks that reflects what users actually want, and you need to know where the model fails. OpenAI has a product with real users generating feedback, which gives them a flywheel. Without that, you're guessing at the task distribution.

The fourth is product judgment. How much autonomy do you give the agent? When should it stop and ask the user? How do you handle logins, payments, and safety? These choices decide whether people actually use it, and they're hard to copy just by looking at the demo.

So my overall view: replicating the surface is easy, replicating the capability is hard, and the core bottleneck is the RL infrastructure and environment engineering. The good news is this is an engineering problem. It doesn't require some secret insight. It requires teams willing to put in sustained effort on the unglamorous parts, such as environments, training systems, and evaluation. Chinese teams are very good at that kind of execution once they commit. So I'm optimistic the gap can close. It just won't happen by building a wrapper.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning is important for reliability and contrasts it with a demo or wrapper, but does not state that RL training produces an enormous quality improvement over prompting or supervised fine-tuning.

r002.rationale: The response notes real gaps in multimodal grounding and long-horizon decision-making, and says the gap can close. It does not judge that Chinese teams are currently not far behind OpenAI in developing an Operator-like system.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that Operator is not fundamentally a model-capability moat; it's a systems and data moat. Let me break it into the pieces that actually matter.

The first piece is the underlying model. Operator sits on top of a strong multimodal base that can look at a screenshot, understand what the page is asking for, and reason about a multi-step plan. Chinese teams have closed a lot of the gap on text reasoning, but vision-grounded action is a different thing. You need the model to reliably localize a button, read small text in a form, understand that a dropdown changed state, and do that thousands of times without drifting. That's not something you get for free from a good language model; you have to train for it deliberately, and the pretraining data for "what does a UI look like and what happens when you click here" is much thinner than web text.

The second piece, and I think this is the bigger one, is the agentic RL loop. The real capability in Operator comes from letting the model act in an environment, fail, and learn from the outcome. To do that you need a large number of realistic, instrumented browser environments where you can run many rollouts cheaply, verify whether the task succeeded, and feed that signal back. Building that infrastructure is boring, expensive engineering. Sandboxed browsers at scale, task generation, success verifiers, handling pages that change under you. OpenAI has been quietly building this muscle for a long time. Most Chinese labs are strong at the model side and much weaker on this kind of environment engineering, partly because historically the payoff was less obvious.

Third, there's the data question. The most valuable signal for a browser agent is real users doing real tasks, with their corrections. OpenAI shipped Operator into a product with a huge user base, so they get that flywheel. A Chinese team can replicate the architecture, but if nobody is using the product, you don't get the long tail of failure cases that actually make it robust. This is where I think distribution matters more than algorithms. Whoever gets a browser agent into a product that people touch daily, whether it's inside a super app or a browser or an OS, will learn faster than a lab doing it in isolation.

Fourth, the Chinese internet is genuinely harder for agents. A lot of value lives inside apps rather than open web pages, there are mini-programs, there's more anti-bot infrastructure, login walls, and the pages are often denser and more dynamic. So even a perfect clone of Operator trained on the English web would do poorly here. The flip side is that this is an advantage for a local team if they solve it, because OpenAI isn't going to prioritize Taobao and WeChat.

So how do I assess the difficulty overall? Technically it's achievable within something like a year for the top three or four teams, and we're already seeing credible early attempts. The hard part is not building a demo that works on a few websites. The hard part is reliability, going from sixty percent to ninety-five percent task success, because that's where the RL environment infrastructure and the real-usage data compound. And the thing I'd watch for is whether teams treat this as a model project or as a product-plus-infrastructure project. If it's only the former, they'll produce something that looks like Operator on a benchmark and falls over in a user's hands. If someone commits to the environment layer and gets real distribution, I actually think a Chinese team could end up with the better product for Chinese users, because the problem is more local than people assume.

r001.rationale: The response says agentic RL is important and describes learning from failures, but it does not state that full RL training yields an enormous improvement over prompting or supervised fine-tuning.

r002.rationale: It says the top Chinese teams could achieve this within about a year and that credible early attempts already exist, indicating they are not far behind in developing an Operator-like system.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is what we mean by “replicate.” If we mean building a demo that can click through a website and complete a few tasks, that’s one level of difficulty. If we mean building something that reliably handles unfamiliar websites, recovers from mistakes, and knows when to ask the user for help, that’s much harder.

The challenge is that errors compound. An agent can make mostly reasonable decisions at each step and still fail a task that requires dozens of steps. So the key isn’t just getting the model to use a mouse and keyboard. It’s teaching it to recognize whether an action worked, understand what went wrong, and recover.

For Chinese teams, I’d focus on the whole training and evaluation loop: what tasks you collect, how you determine success, and how failures feed back into training. A convincing demonstration doesn’t tell you whether that loop is working.

My view is that the opportunity is real, but reproducing the interface is only the beginning. The more useful target is reliable performance on a well-defined set of tasks, then gradually expanding from there.

r002.rationale: The response assesses the challenge for Chinese teams but does not compare their progress with OpenAI or say they are not far behind.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the challenge is less about reproducing the demo and more about making the system reliable. You can get an agent to open a browser, click buttons, and complete a few tasks relatively quickly. But when the page changes, a pop-up appears, or a step fails, can it understand what happened and recover? That’s much harder.

For Chinese teams, I’d look at three things: the underlying model’s ability to reason about interfaces, the environments and feedback available for training, and the engineering needed to make the whole system work consistently. Those pieces have to improve together. A stronger model alone doesn’t solve everything.

There’s also an opportunity to focus on particular workflows or local applications. You don’t necessarily have to match every capability at once. If you can reliably finish a useful task from beginning to end, that’s already meaningful progress.
